core_idea: **Most** either names the greater part of a group on its own, or, with **the**, picks out the single greatest amount when three or more are compared.

senses.definition: used before a plural or uncountable noun, without an article, to mean the greater part of a group or amount
senses.explanation: This **most** talks about people or things in general, not one particular group already mentioned: *most people* means the greater part of people everywhere, not a specific set. It is often followed by **of**: *most of the students*.

examples.text: Most people enjoy a good meal.
Most of the food was gone by the end of the party.
She spends most weekends at home.
Most of my friends live in this city.

senses.definition: used with **the** before a noun to mean the greatest amount or number, when three or more are being compared
senses.explanation: **The most** is the superlative of **more**: it compares three or more amounts and picks out the largest. *She has the most money* compares her with everyone else in the group.

examples.text: Of the three candidates, she has the most experience.
Which team scored the most points?
He has the most patience of anyone I know.

compare.note: **more** compares two amounts; **the most** compares three or more and picks the greatest

phrases.definition: used to mean not more than the amount or number given

examples.text: The trip will take an hour, at most.
We can invite twenty people at most.

usage_note: Without an article, **most** talks about people or things in general: *most cats* means cats in general, not one particular group. With **the**, **most** becomes the superlative of **more** and compares specific amounts: *the most cats* picks out whichever amount is largest among those being compared. **Most** used alone (*most agree*), or before an adjective to form a superlative (*the most difficult*), belongs to separate entries.

learner_errors.note: For a general statement about people or things, no article is used before **most**.

see_also.note: **most** used alone, without a following noun: *most agree*
**most** used before an adjective or adverb to form a superlative: *the most difficult*

adaptation.semantic: **Most** without an article names a general majority; **the most** compares specific amounts and picks the greatest. Many languages use one word for both, so a translator should check which meaning is intended.
